warmup.q: A Kotlin class exposes fun authorizeAsync(req): CompletableFuture<Decision> = scope.future { authorize(req) } to Java. A Java caller adds .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS), and the timeout fires. What happens to the Kotlin coroutine?
options: Nothing: a Java timeout can't reach a Kotlin coroutine
It is cancelled, because the future it belongs to completed
It keeps running, and its result is ignored when it arrives
The JVM interrupts the thread the coroutine runs on
warmup.why: The future returned by future { } is tied to its coroutine: the KDoc says the coroutine is cancelled when the future "is cancelled or otherwise completed". orTimeout completes that same future exceptionally, so the coroutine is cancelled at its next suspension point. Nothing is interrupted, and nothing keeps running.

sections.h: Bridge CompletableFuture both ways with future { } and await()
sections.html:
Most of your Java code speaks CompletableFuture, and kotlinx.coroutines bridges it in both directions with nothing extra on the classpath. The old kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 artifact was merged into the core library in 1.7.

From a future to a suspend call, use await():

Java
// Java equivalent: block a thread on the future, or chain on it
int score = legacyFraudClient.score(req).join();                                  // blocks the caller
CompletableFuture<Decision> d = legacyFraudClient.score(req).thenApply(this::decide);   // or composes
Kotlin
suspend fun fraudScore(req: AuthRequest): Int =
    legacyFraudClient.score(req).await()   // suspends until the future completes; no thread waits

await() suspends without holding a thread. It rethrows the future's exception unwrapped, so you catch the IOException itself rather than an ExecutionException, and it has a fast path for a future that is already done. It also carries cancellation: if the awaiting coroutine is cancelled, it calls future.cancel(false). That is usually right, because nobody wants the answer any more. When the future is shared, or must finish anyway (a capture that has already gone to the issuer), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling it.

From a suspend call to a future, use future { }:

Java
// Java equivalent: the Java caller's side, which is plain CompletableFuture code
CompletableFuture<String> reply = facade.authorizeAsync(req)
    .orTimeout(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .thenApply(decision -> "pay-1: " + decision);
Kotlin
class AuthorizationFacade(private val service: AuthorizationService) : AutoCloseable {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)

    fun authorizeAsync(req: AuthRequest): CompletableFuture<Decision> = scope.future { service.authorize(req) }

    override fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

future { } is a builder like async: it starts a coroutine in the scope and hands its result back as a CompletableFuture. The link runs both ways. A Java caller's cancel(true), or an orTimeout that fires, completes the future, and that cancels the Kotlin coroutine. Give the facade a scope it owns, as in lesson 3 of this track, so closing the facade cancels everything still in flight. GlobalScope.future also compiles, and it leaks in exactly the way lesson 3 described.

try.title: Cancel across the bridge
steps: Read FutureBridge.kt. Predict the three future cancelled lines.
Run the Java twin. It is plain Java calling the Kotlin FraudFacade from the same file, so watch for the [kotlin] lines.
In the Java twin, change orTimeout(50, ...) to orTimeout(500, ...) and run it again. Predict first.

code.title: FutureBridge.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.asDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.future.await import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Kotlin code with a Java-friendly face: every suspend call gets a CompletableFuture twin. */ class FraudFacade : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) suspend fun score(paymentId: String): Int { try { delay(200) // the fraud model return paymentId.length * 7 } catch (e: kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException) { println(" [kotlin] scoring $paymentId was cancelled") throw e } } fun scoreAsync(paymentId: String): CompletableFuture<Int> = scope.future { score(paymentId) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } /** A Java-style future that takes 500 ms, and reports whether someone cancelled it. */ fun slowJavaFuture(): CompletableFuture<String> { val f = CompletableFuture<String>() CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).execute { f.complete("limits loaded") } return f } fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine:") val f1 = slowJavaFuture() launch { f1.await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f1.isCancelled}") println("2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine:") val f2 = slowJavaFuture() launch { f2.asDeferred().await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f2.isCancelled} (it still completes: ${f2.get()})") println("3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it:") FraudFacade().use { facade -> val f3 = facade.scoreAsync("pay-123") delay(50) f3.cancel(true) delay(50) println(" future cancelled: ${f3.isCancelled}") } }

alt.title: FutureBridgeJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FutureBridge.kt, from the Java side: plain Java calling the Kotlin // FraudFacade through its future {} methods. No Continuation, no runBlocking. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class FutureBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (FraudFacade facade = new FraudFacade()) { System.out.println("1. compose two Kotlin calls like any futures:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> total = facade.scoreAsync("pay-1") .thenCombine(facade.scoreAsync("pay-22"), Integer::sum); System.out.println(" combined score: " + total.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); System.out.println("2. a Java timeout cancels the Kotlin coroutine:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> slow = facade.scoreAsync("pay-timeout") .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails the future after 50 ms try { slow.join(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" java caller got: " + e.getCause()); } Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("3. cancel(true) on the future the facade returned:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> cancelled = facade.scoreAsync("pay-cancel"); Thread.sleep(50); cancelled.cancel(true); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println(" future cancelled: " + cancelled.isCancelled()); } } }

try.expect: Case 1 prints future cancelled: true: cancelling the coroutine cancelled the Java future it was awaiting. Case 2 prints false and the future still completes, because asDeferred().await() only waits. Case 3 prints [kotlin] scoring pay-123 was cancelled, then true. In the Java twin, the combined score is 77, and both the orTimeout and the cancel(true) produce a [kotlin] ... was cancelled line. With a 500 ms timeout the 200 ms score finishes first, so there is no timeout and no cancel line for it.

sections.h: Bridge Reactor with mono { }, awaitSingle and asFlow
sections.html:
Reactor speaks Mono and Flux, and the kotlinx-coroutines-reactor module (on this lab's classpath) bridges them.

Java
// Java equivalent: the Reactor side just sees ordinary Mono and Flux values
Mono<Quote> north = quotes.quote(req);                       // built by mono { } in Kotlin
Mono<String> both = Mono.zip(north, quotes.quote(otherReq)).map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2());
Flux<Double> ticks = fx.ticks();                              // a Kotlin Flow through asFlux()
Kotlin
fun quote(req: AuthRequest): Mono<Quote> = mono { quoteSource.quote(req) }      // suspend code as a Mono
suspend fun quoteNow(req: AuthRequest): Quote = webClientQuote(req).awaitSingle() // a Mono in suspend code
fun settlements(): Flow<Batch> = settlementFlux().asFlow()                       // a Flux as a Flow
fun ticks(): Flux<Double> = fxTicks.asFlux()                                     // a Flow as a Flux

mono { } gives a cold Mono: the coroutine starts on subscription, once per subscriber, which is the contract every Reactor user expects (lesson 2 of the reactive track). A null result completes the Mono empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. Its context may not contain a Job ("Mono context cannot contain job in it"), because the subscription owns the coroutine's life, not a scope. flux { } does the same for a stream, with send inside.

In the other direction, awaitSingle() waits for exactly one value and throws NoSuchElementException for an empty Mono; awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. Publisher.asFlow() collects a Flux as a Flow: the Flow's suspension turns into Reactive Streams request(n) demand, and cancelling the collector cancels the subscription. Flow.asFlux() goes back, and the module's README describes the result as TCK-compliant: it passes the Reactive Streams test kit (TCK), which checks a publisher against the spec's numbered rules.

Two things need care. Threads first: unless you pass a dispatcher, mono { } starts its coroutine on Dispatchers.Default, while the Reactor operators around it run wherever their schedulers put them. Then context: Reactor's Context, which WebFlux uses for things like trace ids, is visible inside the coroutine as a ReactorContext element. MDC thread locals are not, for the reason lesson 4 of this track gave.

Quarkus users will meet Mutiny rather than Reactor. The shapes are the same (Uni is a Mono, Multi is a Flux), and Mutiny ships its own Kotlin coroutine bridges.

try.title: Hand a coroutine to Reactor and back
steps: Read ReactorBridge.kt. Predict how many [kotlin] asking north lines print in part 1.
Run the Java twin, which uses the same Kotlin quoteFor and tickFlux functions from plain Reactor code.
In the Kotlin file, change awaitSingle() in part 2 to awaitSingleOrNull() and print the result. Predict first.

code.title: ReactorBridge.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.asFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.awaitSingle import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.asFlux import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.mono import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** A Kotlin suspend call, exposed to Reactor code as a cold Mono. */ fun quoteFor(acquirer: String): Mono<String> = mono { println(" [kotlin] asking $acquirer for a quote") delay(50) if (acquirer == "nobody") null else "$acquirer: 1.80%" } /** A Kotlin Flow of FX ticks, exposed to Reactor code as a Flux. */ fun ticks(): Flow<Double> = flow { for (i in 0 until 5) { delay(20); emit(1.0800 + i / 10_000.0) } } fun tickFlux(): Flux<Double> = ticks().asFlux() fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. mono { } is cold:") val m = quoteFor("north") println(" built the Mono; nothing asked yet") println(" awaitSingle() -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println(" awaitSingle() again -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println("2. an empty Mono:") try { quoteFor("nobody").awaitSingle() } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println(" awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException") } println("3. a Flux consumed as a Flow (cancelling the flow cancels the subscription):") val settlements = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)).map { "batch-$it" }.doOnCancel { println(" [reactor] subscription cancelled") } println(" ${settlements.asFlow().take(3).toList()}") println("4. a Flow handed to Reactor as a Flux:") println(" ${tickFlux().map { "%.4f".format(it) }.collectList().block()}") }

alt.title: ReactorBridgeJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ReactorBridge.kt, from the Java side: Reactor code using the Kotlin // functions through their Mono and Flux faces. The Kotlin side is ReactorBridge.kt. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ReactorBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. the Kotlin Mono is cold, so each subscription asks again:"); Mono<String> north = ReactorBridgeKt.quoteFor("north"); System.out.println(" built the Mono; nothing asked yet"); System.out.println(" block() -> " + north.block()); System.out.println(" block() again -> " + north.block()); System.out.println("2. an empty Mono and a default:"); System.out.println(" " + ReactorBridgeKt.quoteFor("nobody").defaultIfEmpty("no quote: use the default acquirer").block()); System.out.println("3. zip two Kotlin quotes with Reactor operators:"); System.out.println(" " + Mono.zip(ReactorBridgeKt.quoteFor("north"), ReactorBridgeKt.quoteFor("east")) .map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2()).block()); System.out.println("4. a Kotlin Flow as a Flux:"); List<String> ticks = ReactorBridgeKt.tickFlux().map(d -> String.format("%.4f", d)).collectList().block(); System.out.println(" " + ticks); } }

try.expect: [kotlin] asking north prints twice in part 1, once per awaitSingle(), and not when the Mono is built: mono { } is cold. Part 2 throws NoSuchElementException for the empty Mono, and after your change it prints null. Part 3 prints three batches and [reactor] subscription cancelled, because take(3) stopped the Flow. The Java twin shows the same cold Mono from the Reactor side, plus defaultIfEmpty and Mono.zip over two Kotlin quotes.

sections.h: Give Java callers a face they can use
sections.html:
Java can see a suspend function, but it can't call it nicely. The compiler adds a Continuation parameter and changes the return type to Object (lesson 1 of this track showed the bytecode), so from Java the signature looks like this:

Java
// what Java sees for the same function: a Continuation parameter and an Object result
public Object authorize(AuthRequest req, Continuation<? super Decision> $completion)
Kotlin
suspend fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): Decision

You could implement Continuation by hand, but you would be rebuilding a coroutine builder, badly. Give Java callers one of three faces instead.

  • A CompletableFuture method built with future { }, as in this lesson's lab. It is the default for Java code that composes asynchronously, such as a Quarkus REST resource that returns a CompletionStage.
  • A Mono built with mono { }, for code that already lives in Reactor.
  • A blocking method that wraps runBlocking { }, for Java callers that block anyway: a Temporal activity, a JUnit test, a Kafka listener thread, or any code running on a virtual thread. Blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so runBlocking on one is a fair bridge. It is still wrong inside suspend code or on an event-loop thread (lesson 2 of this track).

Whichever you choose, name the faces so the difference shows: authorize for Kotlin, authorizeAsync or authorizeBlocking for Java. Keep the suspend function as the one real implementation and make the others thin wrappers, so the rules for retries and timeouts live in one place. @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and @JvmName take care of the rest of the Java-facing surface: default arguments, companion functions and clashing names.

A blocking face needs a timeout of its own. runBlocking { withTimeout(2.seconds) { authorize(req) } } gives the Java caller an upper bound, and an interrupt of the calling thread cancels the coroutine and makes runBlocking throw InterruptedException. That is the bridge from Java's cancellation model to Kotlin's.

The lab's Java test, JavaCallerTest.java, shows what a Java caller ends up writing against a future { } face: orTimeout, thenApply and get, with no Kotlin types in sight beyond the data classes.

Quick check: two Java callers block on the issuer through different faces, and each caller's thread is interrupted while the call is in flight. Caller A uses authorizeBlocking, the runBlocking face. Caller B calls authorizeAsync(req).get(). Whose issuer call is cancelled? (Only A's. The interrupt reaches runBlocking, which cancels its coroutine. B's interrupt only makes get() throw InterruptedException. The future is still not complete, so the coroutine behind it keeps running until someone cancels the future or closes the facade.)

sections.h: Virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor: choosing for a payments team
sections.html:
All three solve the problem the virtual threads track opened with: a request spends most of its time waiting, and a platform thread per waiting request is too expensive. They solve it at different layers. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so ordinary blocking code scales. Coroutines make waiting explicit with suspend, and add structured concurrency, cancellation and Flow. Reactor turns a request into a pipeline of operators with backpressure. The Try it below runs the same three calls each way, and each takes as long as the slowest call.

Virtual threads (JDK 21+) Kotlin coroutines Reactor
Your code looks like plain blocking Java or Kotlin sequential suspend functions chains of operators
Blocking libraries (JDBC, old SDKs) the natural fit withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a VT dispatcher wrap them, move them to boundedElastic
Fan-out with one deadline StructuredTaskScope, preview in JDK 25 coroutineScope, async, withTimeout Mono.zip, timeout
Cancellation interrupts, if the code checks them flows down the job tree to every child a cancel signal up the chain
Streams with backpressure none built in Flow Flux
Debugging ordinary stacks and thread dumps debug mode and coroutine dumps operator traces, harder to read
Java callers native through future { } or mono { } native

Here is what I would do in a team that writes Quarkus services in Kotlin and Java, talks to Oracle over JDBC, consumes Kafka and runs Temporal workflows.

  • Start with virtual threads for request handling that is mostly blocking calls. Quarkus has @RunOnVirtualThread, JDBC and the Temporal SDK are blocking APIs anyway, and since JDK 24 (JEP 491) synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread in most cases, so JDK 25 is a good base. Cap each downstream with a semaphore or a sized pool (lesson 3 of the virtual threads track).
  • Use coroutines in Kotlin code that needs what virtual threads don't give you: fan-out with one deadline, cancellation that reaches every child, Flow pipelines, StateFlow-style shared state. Blocking calls inside still go through withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher.
  • Keep Reactor (or Mutiny) where a reactive stack already exists, or where you stream with backpressure end to end. Don't start a new, blocking-heavy service on it.

Mixing them is normal, and cheap with the bridges from this lesson. What to avoid is several models in one call path for no reason: a coroutine that calls runBlocking, which calls a Mono, which blocks on JDBC. Pick one model per component, and convert at its edges.

try.title: One request, three ways
steps: Read ThreeWays.kt and its Java twin. Each runs the same three calls (100, 300 and 200 ms) at once. Predict every time.
In ThreeWays.kt, wrap the body of detailsWithCoroutines in withTimeout(250) { ... } and run it again. What happens to the calls still in flight?

code.title: ThreeWays.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis // one payment-details request: account (100 ms), ledger (300 ms) and risk (200 ms), done at once suspend fun detailsWithCoroutines(): List<String> = coroutineScope { val account = async { delay(100); "account" } val ledger = async { delay(300); "ledger" } val risk = async { delay(200); "risk" } listOf(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } /** The same calls written as BLOCKING code, run on whatever dispatcher you pass. */ suspend fun detailsBlocking(vt: CoroutineDispatcher): List<String> = coroutineScope { val account = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(100); "account" } val ledger = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(300); "ledger" } val risk = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(200); "risk" } listOf(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } fun main() = runBlocking { repeat(2) { detailsWithCoroutines() } // warm up val c = measureTimeMillis { println("coroutines: ${detailsWithCoroutines()}") } println(" took $c ms on ${Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @")}") Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> val v = measureTimeMillis { println("blocking code on virtual threads: ${detailsBlocking(vt)}") } println(" took $v ms") } val b = measureTimeMillis { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: ${detailsBlocking(Dispatchers.IO)}") } } println(" took $b ms") }

alt.title: ThreeWaysJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ThreeWays.kt: the same request with virtual threads (plain blocking code) // and with Reactor (operators, no blocking). Same total time: the slowest call. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ThreeWaysJava { static String call(String name, long ms) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(ms); // a blocking client call return name; } static List<String> withVirtualThreads() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> account = vt.submit(() -> call("account", 100)); Future<String> ledger = vt.submit(() -> call("ledger", 300)); Future<String> risk = vt.submit(() -> call("risk", 200)); return List.of(account.get(), ledger.get(), risk.get()); } } static List<String> withReactor() { return Mono.zip( Mono.just("account").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), Mono.just("ledger").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)), Mono.just("risk").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(200))) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())) .block(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { withVirtualThreads(); withReactor(); // warm up long t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("virtual threads: " + withVirtualThreads()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("reactor: " + withReactor()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } }

try.expect: Every version takes about 300 ms: the coroutines, the blocking code on a virtual-thread dispatcher, the blocking code on Dispatchers.IO, the plain virtual threads and the Reactor Mono.zip. With withTimeout(250), the program fails with TimeoutCancellationException at about 250 ms, and the ledger and risk calls still in flight are cancelled with it. Doing that in the Java virtual-thread version would take extra code to cancel the futures yourself.

analogy: Think of three ways to run a busy restaurant. Virtual threads hire a cheap waiter for every table, and each one simply stands there while the kitchen cooks, which is fine because standing costs almost nothing. Coroutines have a few waiters who leave a numbered ticket at each table and come back when the order is ready; they also know which tickets belong to which party, so when a party leaves they tear up all its tickets at once. Reactor runs the room as a conveyor: orders move through fixed stations, and the conveyor only moves as fast as the last station can take plates. The bridges are the pass between the kitchen and the floor, where a ticket can become a plate and back. The analogy breaks on cost: in a real restaurant the conveyor is the expensive option to install, while in code the expensive part of Reactor is the reading, debugging and changing of the pipeline afterwards.
world: In a mixed Kotlin and Java Quarkus codebase, the Kotlin services keep their logic in suspend funs, and each one gets a thin Java face: a CompletionStage method built with future { } for Java resources and the Kafka listener code, and a blocking runBlocking method with its own timeout for Temporal activities, which are blocking by design. Java fraud and limits clients that return CompletableFuture are consumed with await(), so cancelling a payment request also cancels the score request. Where a downstream library is reactive, awaitSingle() and asFlow() bring it in, and mono { } serves a reactive caller. Blocking-heavy Java services, such as a ledger service that is mostly JDBC, move to virtual threads with @RunOnVirtualThread on JDK 25, with a semaphore in front of Oracle's connection pool.
mistake: The most common mistake is bridging with blocking calls: runBlocking { } inside CompletableFuture.supplyAsync to give Java a future, or future.get() (even inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO)) to use a Java future from a coroutine. Both work in a demo, so they ship. Under load, each in-flight call pins a pool thread, and cancellation stops at the bridge: a Java caller's cancel(true) doesn't reach the coroutine, and a cancelled coroutine leaves the Java future running. The fix is the purpose-built bridges, which suspend instead of block and carry cancellation both ways: scope.future { } with a scope you own, future.await(), mono { } and awaitSingle().

compare.title: One fan-out with a deadline: virtual threads vs coroutines

java.title: PaymentDetails.java
java.html: PaymentDetails details(String id) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Account> account = vt.submit(() -> accounts.load(id)); // 1. three blocking calls, Future<List<Entry>> ledger = vt.submit(() -> ledgerClient.recent(id)); // one virtual thread each Future<Risk> risk = vt.submit(() -> riskClient.flags(id)); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(800); try { return new PaymentDetails( // 2. one shared deadline account.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), ledger.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), risk.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException | ExecutionException e) { account.cancel(true); ledger.cancel(true); risk.cancel(true); // 3. cancel by hand throw e; } } // close() waits for every task }

kotlin.title: PaymentDetails.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun details(id: String): PaymentDetails = withTimeout(800) { // 2. one shared deadline coroutineScope { val account = async { accounts.load(id) } // 1. three suspending calls, val ledger = async { ledgerClient.recent(id) } // one coroutine each val risk = async { riskClient.flags(id) } PaymentDetails(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } // 3. a timeout or a failure cancels the other two automatically }

compare.note: Both take as long as the slowest call, and both are cheap: a virtual thread or a coroutine per call. The difference is how much of the structure you write yourself. In Java with virtual threads, the clients can stay blocking, which is the big win, but the shared deadline, the cancel-the-siblings-on-failure step and the cleanup are your code. JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope covers that, but it is still a preview API. In Kotlin, the deadline is withTimeout, the siblings are cancelled by coroutineScope, and the clients must suspend (or be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher). Pick the model that matches your clients: blocking clients favour virtual threads, suspending clients and complex fan-out favour coroutines.

worked.title: Give a Java Temporal activity the Kotlin authorization service

steps.say: The authorization service is Kotlin, and its core is a suspend function with retries and timeouts. A Temporal activity written in Java must call it, and Temporal activities are blocking code. The activity can't call the suspend function directly.
steps.code: class AuthorizationService(private val issuer: IssuerClient) { suspend fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): Decision = retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { issuer.authorize(req) } }

alt.html: // what the Java activity sees: a Continuation parameter it can't sensibly supply public final class AuthorizationService { public final Object authorize(AuthRequest req, Continuation<? super Decision> $completion) { /* ... */ } }

steps.say: Add Java faces in a small Kotlin facade with its own scope. One returns a future, for Java code that composes; one blocks with its own timeout, for callers that block anyway.
steps.code: class AuthorizationJavaApi(private val service: AuthorizationService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // 1. for Java code that composes futures fun authorizeAsync(req: AuthRequest): CompletableFuture<Decision> = scope.future { service.authorize(req) } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound fun authorizeBlocking(req: AuthRequest): Decision = runBlocking { withTimeout(10.seconds) { service.authorize(req) } } override fun close() = scope.cancel() }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same facade, if the service were a Java class returning futures final class AuthorizationJavaApi implements AutoCloseable { private final AuthorizationService service; AuthorizationJavaApi(AuthorizationService service) { this.service = service; } // 1. for Java code that composes futures CompletableFuture<Decision> authorizeAsync(AuthRequest req) { return service.authorizeAsync(req); } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound Decision authorizeBlocking(AuthRequest req) throws Exception { return service.authorizeAsync(req).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } @Override public void close() { } }

steps.say: The activity uses the future face, so it can cancel the Kotlin work when Temporal cancels the activity. Temporal reports a cancel through the heartbeat, which throws.
steps.code: // the activity is Java; this is the Kotlin side it relies on: cancel(true) reaches the coroutine val f = api.authorizeAsync(req) f.cancel(true) // 3. cancels the coroutine inside AuthorizationService, retries included

alt.html: public Decision authorize(AuthRequest req) { CompletableFuture<Decision> f = api.authorizeAsync(req); try { while (true) { try { return f.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException stillWaiting) { Activity.getExecutionContext().heartbeat(null); } // 3. throws if cancelled } } catch (ActivityCompletionException cancelled) { f.cancel(true); // stops the Kotlin coroutine and its retries throw cancelled; } catch (InterruptedException | ExecutionException e) { throw Activity.wrap(e); } }

steps.say: A Reactor-based caller elsewhere gets its own face from the same function, and the retry rules still live in one place.
steps.code: // 4. a cold Mono for reactive callers fun authorizeMono(req: AuthRequest): Mono<Decision> = mono { service.authorize(req) }

alt.html: // 4. the reactive caller's side Mono<Decision> decision = api.authorizeMono(req) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) .onErrorReturn(Decision.DECLINED);

steps.say: Self-check: why not implement authorizeAsync as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { runBlocking { service.authorize(req) } }? (It blocks a common-pool thread for every call, the future has no link to the coroutine so cancel(true) stops nothing, and the work belongs to no scope, so close() can't stop it. That is the bug in this lesson's lab.)

lab.title: Three bridges between Kotlin and Java
steps: Run the tests. Five of ten fail. One test, JavaCallerTest.java, is written in Java, to show what a Java caller of the facade writes.
In AuthorizationFacade.kt, give the class a CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher), return scope.future { authorize(req) } from authorizeAsync, and cancel the scope in close.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: future is an extension on CoroutineScope in kotlinx.coroutines.future. It is in the core library; no extra artifact is needed.
A coroutine cancelled through close() completes its future with a CancellationException, which is what a Java caller sees from get().
mono { } returns Mono<T> from a block that returns T?: a null completes the Mono empty, so the "nobody quotes" test needs no special case.
The stubs' tests wait at most a few seconds each, so a stub never hangs the build. On the solution they finish in milliseconds.
lab.done: All ten tests in JavaInteropTest and JavaCallerTest pass.

drill.title: Three bridges from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class LimitsJavaApi(private val limits: LimitsService) where LimitsService has suspend fun dailyLimit(merchantId: String): Long. Give it fun dailyLimitAsync(merchantId: String): CompletableFuture<Long> for Java and fun dailyLimitMono(merchantId: String): Mono<Long> for Reactor, both cancellable, and a close(). Then write suspend fun MerchantClient.loadAwait(id: String): Merchant for a Java client whose load(id) returns CompletableFuture<Merchant>.

answer.html: class LimitsJavaApi(private val limits: LimitsService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) fun dailyLimitAsync(merchantId: String): CompletableFuture<Long> = scope.future { limits.dailyLimit(merchantId) } fun dailyLimitMono(merchantId: String): Mono<Long> = mono { limits.dailyLimit(merchantId) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } suspend fun MerchantClient.loadAwait(id: String): Merchant = load(id).await()

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: the Java and Reactor callers of those faces class LimitsCaller { private final LimitsJavaApi api; LimitsCaller(LimitsJavaApi api) { this.api = api; } long dailyLimitBlocking(String merchantId) throws Exception { return api.dailyLimitAsync(merchantId).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // blocks this thread: fine on a virtual thread } Mono<String> describe(String merchantId) { return api.dailyLimitMono(merchantId).map(cents -> merchantId + ": " + cents); // cold, cancellable } }

recap: future.await() suspends on a CompletableFuture, unwraps its exception, and cancels the future if the coroutine is cancelled; asDeferred().await() waits without cancelling it.
scope.future { } gives Java a CompletableFuture for suspend code. Cancelling or completing the future cancels the coroutine, and closing the scope cancels everything in flight.
mono { } is a cold Mono (once per subscriber, empty on null, cancelled on dispose). awaitSingle(), asFlow() and asFlux() cover the other directions.
Java can't call a suspend function sensibly. Give it a future face, a Mono face, or a blocking runBlocking face with its own timeout for callers that block anyway.
Virtual threads make blocking code cheap, coroutines add structure, cancellation and Flow, and Reactor gives operator pipelines with backpressure.
Pick one model per component and convert at its edges with the purpose-built bridges, never with runBlocking or get() in the middle of a call path.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks: "We have Kotlin and Java services on Quarkus, Oracle over JDBC, Kafka and Temporal. Should new code use virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor?" Give your answer and the reasons.
explain.answer: For most request handling I'd use virtual threads: our clients are blocking (JDBC, the Temporal SDK, several vendor SDKs), Quarkus can run endpoints on virtual threads, and on JDK 25 the old synchronized pinning problem is mostly gone. We keep plain blocking code and cap each downstream with a semaphore. In Kotlin code where we need more than cheap blocking, like a fan-out with one deadline, cancellation that reaches every child, or Flow pipelines and shared state, I'd use coroutines, and push blocking calls inside them onto Dispatchers.IO or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Reactor or Mutiny stays where it already is or where we genuinely stream with backpressure; I wouldn't start a new blocking-heavy service on it. Where the models meet, we convert at the edge with future {}, await(), mono {} and awaitSingle(), which keep cancellation working, and we never stack runBlocking and blocking get() calls in one call path.

deeper.html:
kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() is the supported route, and it gives every dispatch a fresh virtual thread. That makes it a good home for blocking calls inside coroutines, with two cautions. A coroutine blocked inside it still ignores cancellation unless the call is wrapped in runInterruptible, which interrupts the virtual thread. And the coroutine scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on one worker is lost, so code that relies on thread-local caches gets a new thread every time it resumes.

CompletionStage.await() works for any CompletionStage, not just CompletableFuture, and Deferred.asCompletableFuture() goes the other way for a coroutine you already started with async. On the Reactor side, Deferred.asMono() and Job.asMono() give hot Monos for work that is already running, and Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher() lets coroutines run on a Reactor scheduler, which keeps thread usage in one place in a WebFlux service.

The structured-concurrency story differs most across the three. Coroutines enforce it by default. Virtual threads get it through StructuredTaskScope, a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) whose shape changed between previews. Reactor has no tree of tasks at all, only operator chains that cancel upstream. When you bridge, the tree ends at the bridge: a future { } coroutine belongs to the facade's scope, not to the Java caller, which is exactly why the facade must own and close that scope.
